about: Semitone's mixing and mastering brain: engineer profiles (mix and master, based on how they're known to work; nothing is copied), the best documented profile for each style, how each instrument registers on the spectrum, how parts interact, common problems in plain words with how to find and fix them, destination targets, and the Calibrate workflow. Agreed with Jamie 8 Nov 2026.

engineers.name: Andrew Scheps-style mix
engineers.philosophy: The song comes first: be a fan of it and find its best version. Drums first, the lead vocal last so it fits what's built around it. Lots of shared parallel compression and a rear bus that glues everything except the drums.

moves.what: Shared parallel compression for the drums: one for kick and snare, one for the whole kit, blended under the dry drums
moves.why: Shared compressors make the kit move together

moves.what: A 'rear bus': everything except drums through one glue compressor, blended in
moves.why: Glues the music without squashing the drums

moves.what: Balance the vocal last, after the band is set
moves.why: The vocal fits around the arrangement

moves.what: Use character EQ and saturation when something is wrong, not surgical cuts first

engineers.name: Chris Lord-Alge-style mix
engineers.philosophy: Fast, bright and punchy. All faders up to find the balance, then shape the song in short passes with fader rides more than EQ. Compression mostly moves only a few dB; impact comes from dynamics and rides, not limiting. Mixes quietly.

moves.what: Start with every fader up and balance by ear before processing
moves.why: Balance is most of the mix

moves.what: Ride faders section by section (15–30 seconds at a time) instead of heavier compression
moves.why: Rides keep impact that compression would flatten

moves.what: Brighten guitars around 8 kHz and piano around 5 kHz
moves.why: Bright parts cut through a dense rock mix

moves.what: Add top end to the bass so it still reads when heavy guitars come in
moves.why: The bass's attack carries it in a busy mix

moves.what: Cut the kick's mids and add top to the snare
Fast compression and tempo-synced delays on the vocal, then ride it forward

engineers.name: Tom Elmhirst-style mix
engineers.philosophy: Warmth and feel. The vocal is warm, never harsh, and gets the most time. Problem frequencies are removed with narrow, deep notches found by sweeping. Few effects, chosen for character (springs), and moving with the song. If it feels good, it is good.

moves.what: Find and notch ringing or harsh frequencies on the vocal with narrow cuts
moves.why: Removes what's unpleasant without dulling the voice

moves.what: Two compressors on the vocal: a fast one for peaks, a slow one for level
Carve the midrange where horns, keys and drums compete
A spring-style reverb on drums that rises in the chorus and bridge
moves.why: Space that moves with the song

moves.what: Low-cut instruments that don't need low end (piano, keys)
moves.why: Less mud, more room for bass

engineers.name: Serban Ghenea-style mix
engineers.philosophy: No fixed formula: the song dictates what to do. Find the song's emotional core and maximise it. Polished, precise pop with a clear, controlled lead vocal and tidy de-essing.

moves.what: Careful de-essing and level control on every vocal
Keep the lead above the track at all times, riding words that dip
Push the element that carries the emotion in each section
Tight, mono low end with kick and bass taking turns

engineers.name: Manny Marroquin-style mix
engineers.philosophy: Starts with feeling: is it moody or bright? Mixing is a performance with constant moves of faders, EQ and effects. Natural-sounding results that respect the artist's identity over technical perfection.

moves.what: Set the overall tone from the song's mood (darker for moody, brighter for bright)
Make the mix move: rides on effects and EQ through the song
Leave intentional character (tuning, distortion, timing) alone

engineers.name: Shawn Everett-style mix
engineers.philosophy: Sound as paint: re-amping, tape and saturation to give parts character; the widest range, lowest lows and highest highs both filled. Loudness from balance, not limiting. Parallel drum compression blended with a clean bus.

moves.what: Warm and thicken parts with saturation (tape, drive), darker on the snare
Make sure both the lowest lows and the highest highs are present
Parallel compressed drum bus blended with a clean drum bus
Get loudness from balance so the master needs little limiting

engineers.name: Mike Dean-style mix
engineers.philosophy: Quick passes, keep the session's character, don't reinvent the song. Producer effects on vocals are part of the sound. Familiar tools, big synths and low end.

moves.what: Keep the producer's vocal effects instead of starting clean
moves.why: They're part of the artist's sound

moves.what: Calibrate in short passes, listening fresh each time
Weighty sub, mono and controlled

engineers.name: Alan Meyerson-style score mix
engineers.philosophy: Balance first, then polish. Process stems (groups) rather than single tracks; pan like an orchestra on stage; several reverbs with low and high cuts on the sends; long reverbs to feather note endings; don't build mixes in the middle.

moves.what: Process groups (strings, brass, percussion) instead of single parts
Pan by orchestral seating
Low- and high-cut every reverb send
Longer reverb to feather note endings in slow passages
After setting a process, back it off by about a fifth
moves.why: Leaves room for parts to interact

moves.what: Keep the master below loud pop levels

engineers.name: Bob Katz-style master
engineers.philosophy: Dynamics and calibrated listening. Measure average loudness (the K-System), keep peaks as protection only, and don't chase loudness: louder masters lose quality and fatigue listeners.

moves.what: Master to a K-System scale: K-20 for wide-range music, K-14 for most pop and home listening, K-12 for broadcast
Limit only peaks; aim for a healthy crest factor
Leave headroom so streaming codecs don't distort

engineers.name: Bob Ludwig-style master
engineers.philosophy: Accuracy and translation: master on a flat, accurate system so it sounds right everywhere, from earbuds to car. Compression carries a live performance's energy, but never so much that it sucks the life out.

moves.what: Check on phone, earbuds, car and studio; fix the worst translation first
Keep kick and bass centred; fold low bass to mono
Compression for energy, capped before the life goes

engineers.name: Emily Lazar-style master
engineers.philosophy: Listening first and aligning with the artist's goal. No fixed method: each project shapes the chain. Analogue-style colour and glue (Pultec-style lifts, glue compression); stem mastering when a mix needs help. A clear target and A/B to avoid endless tweaking.

moves.what: Ask what the artist wants (warmer, wider, louder, more like a reference) before touching anything
Broad, musical low and high lifts with a slight dip around 400 Hz
Gentle glue compression across the mix
If one part is the problem, fix it in the stem, not the whole master
Set a target, A/B against it level-matched, and stop when it's met

engineers.name: Randy Merrill-style master (low confidence)
engineers.philosophy: Credits on modern pop (Adele, Ariana Grande, Lady Gaga, Mark Ronson). His methods aren't described in our sources, so this profile uses general modern-pop mastering norms and says so on every card.

moves.what: Competitive but clean pop loudness
moves.why: Holds up next to current pop (stand-in)

moves.what: Clear top end, controlled low end

house.name: Semitone house profile
house.philosophy: Mixing and mastering best practice for the genre, used where no engineer profile is researched yet. Says so on every card.

bands.means: felt more than heard; kick and bass fundamentals
clarity and attack; the ear's most sensitive zone

harmony.tip: thinner and darker than the lead

chords.tip: carve 2–3 dB where the vocal lives

counter.tip: slightly darker or different register than the lead

bass.dyn: compress for even level; mono below 120 Hz

bass2.tip: only one part owns the sub; high-pass the other

drums.kick: 50–80 Hz thump, 2–5 kHz click, cut 300–500 Hz box

loop.highpass: 150 Hz unless it's a bass or drum loop

returns.band: cut below 150–200 Hz and above 8–10 kHz on reverb returns

fix: sidechain the bass 2–3 dB from the kick
complementary EQ: dip the bass where the kick peaks
dynamic EQ dip on the other part only while the vocal sings (−2 to −4 dB)
high-pass the pad higher; one part owns the warmth
one owns the sub; the other high-passed above 120 Hz
harmony darker and de-essed harder; pan the stack

interactions.zone: sum of all parts in 200–400 Hz
fix: find the parts adding most and trim the least important

problems.usually: Too much 200–500 Hz summed across many parts.
problems.find: Measure each part's energy in 200–500 Hz while the mix plays; list the top contributors and where in the song it builds up.
fixes: high-pass parts that don't need lows
dip 250–400 Hz on the 2 biggest contributors (−2 to −4 dB)
problems.limits: max −6 dB per band; never on the lead without asking

problems.usually: Sub and bass energy too high or uncontrolled; often kick and bass fighting.
problems.find: Low-band level vs genre target; kick/bass overlap.
fixes: sidechain or complementary EQ kick vs bass

problems.usually: Missing 100–250 Hz, or over-high-passed parts.
problems.find: Compare low-mid energy with the genre target; find over-eager high-passes.
fixes: gentle shelf on the main body part

problems.usually: Resonance in 400 Hz–1.2 kHz.
problems.find: Sweep for narrow peaks on the suspected part.
fixes: narrow cut on the resonance (−3 to −6 dB)

problems.usually: Peaks in 2.5–5 kHz, often from several bright parts or a resonance.
problems.find: Find narrow peaks and summed energy 2–5 kHz; flag the loudest contributors.
fixes: dynamic EQ on the peak (acts only when it's loud)
dip competing parts, not the vocal

problems.usually: Sibilance 5–9 kHz on vocals, harmonies or hats.
problems.find: Detect s/t events on vocal parts; measure peak vs body.
fixes: de-ess the part (3–6 dB on the s only)
darken harmonies more than the lead

problems.usually: Not enough 8–16 kHz, or masking up top.
problems.find: Air-band energy vs genre target.
fixes: gentle high shelf on the master or the key parts

problems.usually: Vocal too low or masked in 1–4 kHz.
problems.find: Vocal-to-music level; masking partners in 1–4 kHz.
fixes: dynamic dips on masking parts while the vocal sings
problems.limits: never above the genre's vocal level

problems.usually: Vocal level above genre target or too dry.
problems.find: Vocal-to-music level vs target.

problems.usually: Too many parts in the same register and time.
problems.find: part-roles crowd and mask checks.
fixes: mute or thin the least important part in that section

problems.usually: Transients squashed or masked; kick/snare too low.
problems.find: Crest factor on drums; transient level vs body.
fixes: transient emphasis on kick and snare

problems.usually: Over-compression or limiting.
problems.find: Crest factor, gain reduction totals per bus and master.
problems.limits: master crest ≥ 6 dB pop, ≥ 8 dB others

problems.usually: Out-of-phase stereo content; wide lows.
problems.find: Correlation meter; mono fold-down loss per part.

problems.usually: Everything panned centre, no stereo effects.
problems.find: Stereo image width.

problems.usually: Reverb too long/loud or low-mid heavy.
problems.find: Reverb return level and decay vs tempo.
fixes: shorter decay timed to the tempo

problems.usually: A narrow resonance.
problems.find: Sweep for sustained narrow peaks.

problems.usually: Plosive low-frequency bursts on vocals.
problems.find: Detect low-frequency transients on vocal takes.
fixes: dynamic high-pass on the p only

problems.usually: Background noise, mains hum or edit clicks.
problems.find: Noise floor in gaps; 50/60 Hz harmonics; discontinuities.

problems.usually: Section levels or vocal level vary too much.
problems.find: Section loudness vs the energy curve.
problems.limits: follow the emotion curve, not flatten it

problems.usually: Mix depends on studio speakers (low end, width, harshness).
problems.find: Listen-on simulations: phone, earbuds, car, laptop.

problems.usually: Master below destination target.
problems.find: Integrated LUFS vs target.
fixes: more limiting up to the target with crest guard
problems.limits: stop at the target; streaming turns loud masters down

problems.usually: Over-limited or clipping.
problems.find: True peak, inter-sample overs, distortion detection.

stream.name: Streaming
stream.note: platforms turn loud masters down; dynamics win

calibrate.about: Mix it for me / Master it for me: pressed by the user only. Runs the steps below with the chosen engineer profile as the weighting (like producer passes), produces a list of changes with reasons, a level-matched A/B, and keeps the user's manual choices.
steps: gain staging: every part peaks around −18 to −10 dBFS before processing
cleanup: high-passes by role, plosives, noise, resonances
interactions: masking pairs and the summed mud and harsh zones (interactions above)
tone: each part toward its role's target, the whole mix toward the genre's tonal curve
dynamics: compression and de-essing by role, bus glue by the engineer's style
space: returns, panning, width, mono low end
rides: section and vocal rides from the emotion curve
master (Master it): tonal balance vs genre curve, glue, limiter to the destination, true peak, translation checks
rules: level-match A/B so louder never fools the ear
never touch what the user locked (🔒 on a band, strip or bus)
each change is a switchable item with its reason and the engineer layer that led
max change per pass: ±6 dB EQ per band, 6 dB gain reduction per compressor; bigger needs a click
explain in plain words and show where in the spectrum and the song
re-run is incremental: only changes what moved since last time
